title: Metals, Alloys and Metallurgy

cards.h: The Iron Age is still on
cards.b: Bridges, cars, wires, coins, cookware, implants: metals underpin civilisation. Most metals sit in the ground as ores (compounds), and turning them into useful metal is metallurgy. Human history is even named after metals: Bronze Age, Iron Age.

Metals are shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (hammer into sheets) and ductile (draw into wires). The metallic bond, a sea of free electrons, explains all of this. Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature; sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife.

From most to least reactive: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Ag, Au.

  • Reactive metals (K, Na) react with cold water: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2.
  • Middle metals react with acids.
  • Gold and silver barely react, which is why gold is found native and is prized.

A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu.

The ore is concentrated first. Then:

Roasting heats sulphide ores in air; calcination heats carbonates in limited air; smelting reduces an oxide to metal.

Haematite (Fe2O3), coke (carbon) and limestone go in the top; hot air goes in at the bottom.

  • C + O2 → CO2, then CO2 + C → 2CO
  • Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2
  • Limestone makes slag: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, then CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3, which floats and removes impurities.

Aluminium is too reactive for carbon: Hall and Héroult (1886) electrolysed alumina dissolved in molten cryolite.

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers, so layers slide less: alloys are usually harder and stronger.

  • Steel: iron with 0.2 to 2 percent carbon.
  • Stainless steel: iron, chromium (about 10.5 percent or more), nickel.
  • Brass: copper and zinc. Bronze: copper and tin.
  • Solder: tin and lead (now often lead-free).

How much iron from 160 kg of Fe2O3? Molar mass Fe2O3 = 2 x 56 + 3 x 16 = 160 g/mol. So 160 kg = 1,000 mol. Equation gives 2 mol Fe per mole Fe2O3, so 2,000 mol Fe = 2,000 x 56 g = 112 kg.

Which displaces which? Zinc and copper sulphate: zinc is higher in the series, so Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu works. Copper in zinc sulphate does not.

• Reactive does not mean quick to decay. Aluminium forms a protective oxide film, which is why it lasts.
  • Steel is not pure iron.
  • Alloys are mixtures, not compounds, though they can contain compounds.
  • Rust is not the same as all corrosion. Silver tarnishes by forming sulphide, copper turns green with a carbonate layer.

• The Delhi iron pillar: about 7 m tall, around 6 tonnes, made of nearly pure wrought iron (about 98 percent) in roughly the 4th to 5th century CE (associated with Gupta king Chandragupta II). It has stayed largely rust-free for about 1,600 years.
  • Wootz steel from southern India, high in carbon, was exported and became legendary as Damascus steel.
  • Zawar in Rajasthan is one of the world's earliest sites of zinc distillation.
  • Tata Steel began producing at Jamshedpur in 1912 (company founded 1907).

• Extraction method depends on reactivity: carbon reduction for mid metals, electrolysis for reactive ones.
  • Blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2.
  • Alloys are stronger because mixed atoms block sliding layers.

Think about it

1. Why can't aluminium be extracted by heating with carbon?

2. Why do we add carbon to iron to make steel, but not too much?
